_about: Mental Health Support question bank: 60 per part, 10 per room. rooms[r] = [pool for object 1, pool for object 2], 5 questions each; every game picks 1 from each pool (12 per game). In the Bedroom, pool 1 = crisis openers, pool 2 = safety follow-ups. setbacks = the two bad-day events. Each option: g (help/okay/hurt), t (answer), why, re (reply), optional say (spoken line).

rooms.title: Spotting the red flags
rooms.scene: For weeks, {p} has ditched movie nights, hibernated until noon, and completely ignored {their} guitar.
rooms.ask: What is your tactical opening move?

opts.t: Catch {them} in a quiet moment and say neutrally: “I've noticed your routine shifted a lot lately. How are you holding up beneath the surface?”
opts.why: Spotting lifestyle shifts without weaponizing them opens a low-pressure gateway for honesty.
opts.re: Honestly? Not great. I feel like I'm moving through thick mud every day, but... thanks for noticing without making a big deal out of it.
opts.say: I've noticed your routine shifted a lot lately. How are you holding up beneath the surface?

opts.t: Grab a board game: “Come on, let's play a quick round together—just the two of us, to unwind.”
opts.why: Even micro-social obligations can feel like an impossible performance requirement when someone's battery is drained.
opts.re: I know you're trying to help, but looking at a board and making decisions right now just feels like another chore I'm going to fail at.

opts.t: Mention casually: “You haven't touched that guitar in weeks.”
opts.why: Bare observations of skipped habits subtly point out their decline, creating quiet pressure and self-consciousness.
opts.re: Right. Because staring at it makes me feel even more useless. Thanks for keeping score.
opts.say: You haven't touched that guitar in weeks.

rooms.title: Reading the subtext
rooms.scene: You spot {p} slouching on the sofa under a blanket with noise-canceling headphones on, offering a microscopic, strained smile before looking at the floor.
rooms.cue: 🎧 Cocooned in a blanket burrito, eyes locked downward.
rooms.line: Oh, hey. Just chilling, totally living my best lazy Sunday life.
rooms.ask: Read the subtext. What's the optimal play here?

opts.t: Sit down a safe distance away and murmur: “Mind if I occupy space near you in absolute silence? Zero conversation required on your end.”
opts.why: Their brain capacity is maxed out. Quiet presence respects boundaries while proving they aren't stranded.
opts.re: Yeah. You can sit there. Just... don't ask me any questions, okay?
opts.say: Mind if I occupy space near you in absolute silence? Zero conversation required on your end.

opts.t: Smile warmly: “No pressure to talk, but I'm going to put your favorite comfort show on softly.”
opts.why: Introducing external sensory stimuli forces an exhausted nervous system to process data when it needs static reduction.
opts.re: Please turn it off. The noise is just bouncing around inside my head right now.
opts.say: No pressure to talk, but I'm putting your favorite show on softly for some gentle company.

opts.t: Look at the headphones and say: “Quiet day.”
opts.why: Using clipped minimalism to comment on withdrawal isolates them further by highlighting detachment without warmth.
opts.re: Yeah. Thrilling life I've got here.
opts.say: Quiet day.

rooms.title: The 'I'm Just Tired' Mask
rooms.scene: {P} has replied 'just tired' every single evening for three weeks while visibly losing weight and skipping tasks.
rooms.line: Seriously, I just didn't sleep great last night. Stop looking at me like that.
rooms.ask: How do you respond without triggering defensiveness?

opts.t: Soften your posture: “Fair enough, I'll back off. Just know if it ever turns out to be heavier than bad sleep, you don't have to carry it solo.”
opts.why: Respecting stated boundaries while leaving an unpressured door open preserves trust without forcing a confession.
opts.re: Fine. Whatever. Just... leave it alone for tonight.
opts.say: Fair enough, I'll back off. Just know if it ever turns out to be heavier than bad sleep, you don't have to carry it solo.

opts.t: “I'm only looking because I care—let me order you some melatonin and blackout curtains to fix your sleep.”
opts.why: Jumping straight into logistical problem-solving bypasses the emotional reality behind exhaustion.
opts.re: I don't need your melatonin or your fixes. I just need you to stop analyzing every single thing I do.
opts.say: I'm only looking because I care—let me order you some melatonin and blackout curtains to fix your sleep.

opts.t: “You said the exact same thing yesterday.”
opts.why: Directly tracking and repeating past statements turns dialogue into a scoreboard, shutting down future disclosure.
opts.re: Oh, I'm sorry, is there a daily quota of new excuses I'm supposed to meet for you?
opts.say: You said the exact same thing yesterday.

rooms.title: Cancelled Plans Pattern
rooms.scene: Ten minutes before a small dinner with close friends, {p} texts from the bed asking you to go alone and make up an excuse.
rooms.line: Tell them I have a migraine. I just can't put a face on tonight.
rooms.ask: What is your immediate move before leaving?

opts.t: Knock softly, peek in without lecturing: “I'll cover for you, no problem. Want me to bring back soup later, or leave it outside your door?”
opts.why: Removing social guilt and offering zero-demand care protects their dignity during an energy crash.
opts.re: Just leave it outside the door. Thank you... I'm really sorry about tonight.
opts.say: I'll cover for you, no problem. Want me to bring back soup later, or leave it outside your door?

opts.t: Sit on the edge of the mattress: “I won't force you, just promise me you'll step outside for ten minutes while I'm gone.”
opts.why: Attaching wellness homework to a cancelled plan turns rest into another obligation they might fail.
opts.re: Great, now even staying home comes with homework. Just go have fun without me.
opts.say: I won't force you, just promise me you'll step outside for ten minutes while I'm gone.

opts.t: Reply: “I'll tell them you stayed home.”
opts.why: Neutral compliance delivers social news without support or warmth, leaving them to sit alone in isolation.
opts.re: Whatever. Tell them whatever you want.
opts.say: I'll tell them you stayed home.

rooms.title: The Sudden Silence
rooms.scene: Standing by the counter preparing lunch, {p} goes completely mute mid-sentence and stares blankly out the window.
rooms.cue: 👀 Shoulders slumped, jaw clenched, fingers stiff on the edge of the counter.
rooms.ask: How do you handle the sudden shift?

opts.t: Lower your voice slightly and say gently: “No rush to talk—we can just stand in quiet until you're ready.”
opts.why: Lowering sensory demand and removing conversational pressure lets their nervous system regulate safely.
opts.re: Thanks... my head just sort of short-circuited for a second there.
opts.say: No rush to talk—we can just stand in quiet until you're ready.

opts.t: Reach over and pat {their} arm: “Hey, where did your brain just go? Tell me what just popped into your head.”
opts.why: Demanding immediate verbalization when someone dissociates or hits a wave of numbness overwhelms them.
opts.re: Nowhere! Stop interrogating me every time I zone out for two seconds.
opts.say: Hey, where did your brain just go? Tell me what just popped into your head.

opts.t: Keep wiping the counter: “Lunch is almost ready. Can you grab the plates?”
opts.why: Carrying on with chores and small talk while they shut down treats their sudden withdrawal like it isn't happening.
opts.re: Plates? I just… I can't right now. Never mind.

rooms.title: Brain Fog & Indecision
rooms.scene: You ask {p} what {they} want{s} to watch, and {they} freeze{s} for forty seconds, visibly distressed over choosing between two options.
rooms.line: I don't know. Why is picking a show making me want to cry right now?
rooms.ask: How do you relieve decision paralysis?

opts.t: Take the wheel calmly: “Decision fatigue is real. I'm putting on this movie—all you have to do is sit down.”
opts.why: Executive dysfunction makes trivial choices feel crushing; removing micro-decisions restores calm immediately.
opts.re: Thank you... honestly, making that choice felt like trying to climb a brick wall.
opts.say: Decision fatigue is real. I'm putting on this movie—all you have to do is sit down.

opts.t: Smile encouragingly: “Take a deep breath! Let's flip a coin so you can practice quick low-stakes choices.”
opts.why: Turning cognitive overload into a 'skill-building exercise' misses that their brain is genuinely depleted.
opts.re: I don't want to flip a coin, I just want someone to decide so my brain can stop whirring.
opts.say: Take a deep breath! Let's flip a coin so you can practice quick low-stakes choices.

opts.t: Wait with the remote: “Take your time. I'll just stand here until you pick.”
opts.why: Standing over someone and waiting while their brain is frozen adds pressure and makes them feel even more inadequate.
opts.re: Don't just stand there waiting on me! Just pick something already.

rooms.title: Mounting Clutter
rooms.scene: Papers and notes have sat stacked in an unorganized pile on the desk for weeks, and {p} is staring at it looking defeated.
rooms.line: I can't even sort a stack of notes. What is actually wrong with me?
rooms.ask: What is the most supportive intervention?

opts.t: Sit on the chair beside the desk: “Depression turns small tasks into mountains. Want to just toss the junk in the bin together?”
opts.why: Lowering the standard and normalizing executive dysfunction removes shame.
opts.re: Yes, please. I've been staring at this pile for three days feeling completely frozen.
opts.say: Depression turns small tasks into mountains. Want to just toss the junk in the bin together?

opts.t: “You're just overwhelmed—set a fifteen-minute timer and sort just the top folder for a quick dopamine win!”
opts.why: Productivity hacks assume normal energy reserves and often leave depressed individuals feeling worse if they stall.
opts.re: A timer isn't going to magically give me energy I don't have. Just leave it.
opts.say: You're just overwhelmed—set a fifteen-minute timer and sort just the top folder for a quick dopamine win!

opts.t: Reach past the pile for a book: “Everyone gets messy sometimes. It's just paper.”
opts.why: Physical avoidance of the clutter while bypassing the person reinforces feelings of being an invisible obstacle.
opts.re: Right, step right over it. It's not just paper to me.

rooms.title: Short, Flat Replies
rooms.scene: All week, {p}'s notes in your shared journal have shrunk to one-word answers, a sharp drop from expressive entries.

opts.t: Leave a low-friction note: “Hey, noticing your entries have been brief lately. Zero need to write a paragraph—just thinking of you.”
opts.why: Explicitly removing the obligation to reply prevents check-ins from becoming another unread chore.
opts.re: Thanks for not pushing. I'll write more when my head clears up.
opts.say: Hey, noticing your entries have been brief lately. Zero need to write a paragraph—just thinking of you.

opts.t: Write back: “You've seemed really distant this week—did something happen between us or are you having a rough patch?”
opts.why: Asking whether you caused the distance forces them to expend scarce energy reassuring you.
opts.re: Nothing happened between us. Can we stop analyzing my journal entries?
opts.say: You've seemed really distant this week—did something happen between us or are you having a rough patch?

opts.t: Write back one line: “Got it. Talk when you feel like it.”
opts.why: A short, flat reply to short, flat entries ends the conversation and quietly accepts the distance.
opts.re: Got it? Really? That's all you've got for me?

rooms.title: Hygiene Slippage
rooms.scene: You notice {p} has worn the same sweatpants for four days straight and hasn't brushed {their} hair.
rooms.ask: How do you offer gentle care without embarrassing {them}?

opts.t: Run a warm shower, lay out a clean towel and fresh hoodie without commentary, and say: “Bathroom's open if you want a reset—no pressure.”
opts.why: Setting up the environment quietly eliminates activation steps without drawing attention to appearance.
opts.re: Okay... thank you. I'll go take a warm shower in a minute.
opts.say: Bathroom's open if you want a reset—no pressure.

opts.t: Hand {them} a fresh outfit with a bright smile: “Come on, a hot shower will make you feel brand new!”
opts.why: Promising that basic hygiene will transform mood sets up unrealistic expectations and subtle judgment.
opts.re: A shower isn't magic, it's just exhausting. Leave me alone.
opts.say: Come on, a hot shower will make you feel brand new!

opts.t: Leave a towel on the bed: “Just putting this here in case you want it.”
opts.why: Placing a bathroom item down without context creates unspoken behavioral prompting.
opts.re: Stop leaving passive-aggressive hints about my hygiene around the room.

rooms.title: Returning from Work
rooms.scene: {P} comes home from work, drops {their} bag, and sits down staring at the floor without moving.
rooms.line: I spent eight hours pretending to be a functional human. I have nothing left.

opts.t: Pour a glass of water and slide it over quietly: “You don't have to perform here. Take all the quiet time you need.”
opts.why: Acknowledging exhaustion and offering immediate physical comfort signals total safety.
opts.re: God, thank you. I am so tired of smiling at people all day.
opts.say: You don't have to perform here. Take all the quiet time you need.

opts.t: “You did great getting through the day! Let's talk through what drained you most today.”
opts.why: Immediately asking them to recount stressors demands mental labor right when their tank hits zero.
opts.re: I don't want to talk about work right now, I just want silence.
opts.say: You did great getting through the day! Let's talk through what drained you most today.

opts.t: Flip through the mail: “Long day for everyone, honestly. Did the electric bill come?”
opts.why: Stepping past someone sitting in heavy depletion to check mail communicates that routine tasks outrank their state.
opts.re: Yeah, check the bill. That's definitely more important than me standing here.

rooms.title: Stealthy acts of service
rooms.scene: {P} hasn't eaten in twelve hours and is staring down a piece of plain toast like it requires advanced calculus.

opts.t: Make something simple, set it nearby and sit down: “I made too much—help yourself if you want.”
opts.why: Depression makes basic tasks feel mountainous. Quiet, low-friction help removes barriers without pressure.
opts.re: Thanks... I couldn't figure out how to start eating, but I'll try a bit of this.

opts.t: Cut the toast into neat pieces and prompt: “Eat just three bites for me, okay? You'll feel better once blood sugar rises.”
opts.why: Setting micro-goals shifts focus to performance and creates a failure condition if they still can't eat.
opts.re: Stop treating me like a toddler. I'll eat if I'm hungry.
opts.say: Eat just three bites for me, okay? You'll feel better once blood sugar rises.

opts.t: Head for the door: “I'll leave you to it. Shout if you need anything.”
opts.why: Leaving the room while someone struggles with basic eating leaves them entirely alone with it.
opts.re: Great, walk away. Leave me staring at food I can't touch.

rooms.title: Countering the Burden Trap
rooms.scene: While scrubbing plates together by the sink, {p} stops dead, staring blankly at the soapy water.
rooms.line: I'm so sorry. I am genuinely just a massive anchor dragging your entire life down.
rooms.ask: How do you counter this emotional trap?

opts.t: Look {them} straight in the eye: “You aren't an anchor. We're riding out a brutal storm, and I'm right here in this boat with you voluntarily.”
opts.why: Feeling like a burden is a hallmark symptom of depression. Direct, unconditional reassurance cuts through distortion.
opts.re: Do you really mean that? I'm just so scared I'm ruining things for you.
opts.say: You aren't an anchor. We're riding out a brutal storm, and I'm right here in this boat with you voluntarily.

opts.t: Hold {their} wet hands gently: “I won't pretend this season hasn't stretched me thin—but I love you enough to push through.”
opts.why: Admitting how taxing they are right when they feel worthless confirms their darkest fear.
opts.re: See? I knew I was just a burden to you. I'm sorry.
opts.say: I won't pretend this season hasn't stretched me thin—but I love you enough to push through.

opts.t: Keep scrubbing: “Don't be silly. Pass me that pan?”
opts.why: Maintaining rhythmic chores through a vulnerable self-deprecation statement signals emotional detachment.
opts.re: Yeah, keep washing plates. Ignore what I just said, like always.

rooms.title: Administrative Overwhelm
rooms.scene: A stack of unopened mail and an overdue bill reminder sit untouched on the desk.
rooms.line: If I open those envelopes, I'm going to panic. I'm failing at basic adulthood.
rooms.ask: How do you support {them} without taking over {their} autonomy?

opts.t: Pull up a chair beside {them}: “Want to sit together while I open the mail and sort junk, and we only look at one real letter?”
opts.why: Body-doubling and breaking down tasks preserves agency while sharing cognitive load.
opts.re: That would actually help so much. I feel like I'm drowning in paper.
opts.say: Want to sit together while I open the mail and sort junk, and we only look at one real letter?

opts.t: Scoop up the stack: “Give those to me—I'll pay everything and handle your inbox from now on.”
opts.why: Over-functioning and stripping away all responsibility reinforces helplessness and breeds resentment.
opts.re: No, don't take over everything, that just makes me feel completely useless.
opts.say: Give those to me—I'll pay everything and handle your inbox from now on.

opts.t: Tidy the stack into the organizer: “There—now it's out of sight. Problem solved.”
opts.why: Hiding the mail without asking bypasses their say in it and confirms their fear of being inadequate.
opts.re: Don't touch my desk. I can handle my own mess eventually.

rooms.title: Insomniac Spiral
rooms.scene: At 2:30 AM, {p} is wide awake scrolling on {their} phone after lying in the dark for hours.
rooms.line: My brain refuses to shut off and tomorrow is already ruined.

opts.t: Keep your voice low and calm: “Resting your body still counts. Want me to play a boring sleep podcast softly?”
opts.why: Removing pressure to force sleep reduces performance anxiety that keeps insomnia alive.
opts.re: Please do. My brain won't stop running in circles.
opts.say: Resting your body still counts. Want me to play a boring sleep podcast softly?

opts.t: “Put your phone away right now—blue light ruins melatonin and we need to fix your sleep hygiene.”
opts.why: Lecturing on sleep hygiene at 2:30 AM feels corrective rather than soothing.
opts.re: Lecturing me at 2:30 AM is not helping me sleep, it's making me anxious.
opts.say: Put your phone away right now—blue light ruins melatonin and we need to fix your sleep hygiene.

opts.t: Roll over: “Can you turn the brightness down? Some of us have work tomorrow.”
opts.why: Physical shielding against screen glow communicates sleep-disruption annoyance without words.
opts.re: Fine, keep the blanket. Way to make me feel unwelcome in bed.

rooms.title: Declining Help Out of Guilt
rooms.scene: You offer to pick up {p}'s prescription, and {they} immediately tense up on the couch.
rooms.line: No, stop doing things for me. You're already doing everything and I feel pathetic.
rooms.ask: How do you reframe accepting help?

opts.t: Keep it light and equal: “I'm driving past the pharmacy anyway—let me grab it so we both get an easier evening.”
opts.why: Framing help as ordinary convenience rather than charity protects dignity and lowers guilt.
opts.re: If you're already going anyway... okay. Thank you.
opts.say: I'm driving past the pharmacy anyway—let me grab it so we both get an easier evening.

opts.t: “You shouldn't feel pathetic—when you're sick, it's my job to take care of everything.”
opts.why: Casting them as 'sick' and yourself as sole caretaker can deepen dependency.
opts.re: I'm not sick, I'm broken. Stop calling it sick.
opts.say: You shouldn't feel pathetic—when you're sick, it's my job to take care of everything.

opts.t: Set your keys down: “Okay, suit yourself. I won't offer again.”
opts.why: Withdrawing the offer the moment they hesitate closes the door instead of reassuring them.
opts.re: Whatever. Fine. Don't help me then.

rooms.title: Sensory Overload
rooms.scene: After a loud morning outside, {p} sits on the rug, breathing shallowly with hands over {their} ears.
rooms.cue: 👀 Shoulders hunched against ambient apartment noises.
rooms.line: There's too much noise. I can't process anything.

opts.t: Mute the TV smoothly: “Totally fine. Go lie down somewhere quiet—I'll close all the doors and check on you later.”
opts.why: Providing an immediate, zero-shame exit route stops sensory overload from escalating.
opts.re: Thank you... the noise was literally making my chest tighten up.
opts.say: Totally fine. Go lie down somewhere quiet—I'll close all doors and check on you later.

opts.t: “Just breathe slowly with me—if we sit here through the noise, you'll prove you can handle it.”
opts.why: Forcing exposure therapy in the middle of acute overwhelm prioritizes conquest over safety.
opts.re: I can't handle it, I told you! Stop making me stay in this room!
opts.say: Just breathe slowly with me—if we sit here through the noise, you'll prove you can handle it.

opts.t: Hold the remote: “It's not that loud. Give it a minute—you'll get used to it.”
opts.why: Pausing passively during acute sensory overload leaves them stranded inside the triggering environment.
opts.re: I can't get used to it! Turn it off, please!

rooms.title: Morning Coffee Ritual
rooms.scene: You wake up early and see {p} sitting at the table staring at an empty mug, too drained to boil water.
rooms.ask: How do you practice stealthy care?

opts.t: Make two mugs of tea and slide one over: “Extra one. No need to talk.”
opts.why: Anticipating a small comfort quietly delivers warmth without asking for social energy.
opts.re: Thanks... I couldn't manage boiling water today. This is really kind.

opts.t: Bring over a mug and ask warmly: “Rough night? Rate your energy from one to ten.”
opts.why: Requiring self-assessment metrics first thing in the morning turns support into clinical tracking.
opts.re: I'm not doing a morning evaluation checklist. Just let me drink in peace.
opts.say: Rough night? Rate your energy from one to ten.

opts.t: Pour your own coffee: “Morning. Kettle's there if you want some.”
opts.why: Making your own beverage while ignoring their empty cup highlights the solitude of their struggle.
opts.re: Yeah, get your own and leave me sitting here with an empty cup.

rooms.title: Getting Outside
rooms.scene: {P} hasn't stepped outside in five days.
rooms.line: The thought of walking around the block feels like climbing Everest.
rooms.ask: How do you adjust the goal?

opts.t: Open the door wide: “Forget the walk. Want to just stand by the open door in our socks for sixty seconds?”
opts.why: Shrinking the threshold to zero-effort contact respects limits while breaking stagnation.
opts.re: Just the door? Yeah... I think I can manage that without panicking.
opts.say: Forget the walk. Want to just stand by the open door in our socks for sixty seconds?

opts.t: “That's why we start small—let's lace up sneakers and commit to one lap around the building.”
opts.why: Even a single lap requires getting dressed and being seen, which may exceed current capacity.
opts.re: No, a lap is too much. I can't go outside today.
opts.say: That's why we start small—let's lace up sneakers and commit to one lap around the building.

opts.t: Put on your jacket: “Fair enough. I'm going for a walk—fresh air helps me.”
opts.why: Leaving for fresh air by yourself while your partner remains inside emphasizes stagnation.
opts.re: Great, go enjoy the fresh air while I rot inside.

rooms.title: Gift of Presence
rooms.scene: You bring home {p}'s favorite takeout, and {they} look{s} guilty.
rooms.line: You shouldn't spend money on me when I haven't reciprocated.
rooms.ask: How do you diffuse transactional guilt?

opts.t: Set bags down casually: “Relationships aren't a scoreboard. Sometimes it's 80/20, and I'm happy to cover the 80.”
opts.why: Dismantling scorekeeping relieves pressure to 'earn' care while depressed.
opts.re: I hate that you have to carry so much of the weight right now. But thank you.
opts.say: Relationships aren't a scoreboard. Sometimes it's 80/20, and I'm happy to cover the 80.

opts.t: “Don't worry about paying me back—once you're feeling better, you can treat me to dinner!”
opts.why: Promising future payback still keeps the interaction on a transactional ledger.
opts.re: It's still a debt hanging over my head. I hate feeling like I owe you.
opts.say: Don't worry about paying me back—once you're feeling better, you can treat me to dinner!

opts.t: Set the bag and receipt down: “It's fine. We can sort out who owes what later.”
opts.why: Leaving financial documentation next to a gift turns care into an itemized transaction ledger.
opts.re: Did you really have to leave the itemized receipt right there for me to look at?

rooms.title: Work Performance Anxiety
rooms.scene: {P} has fallen behind on work tasks and is paralyzed by dread.
rooms.line: If I open my laptop, I'm going to see overdue notifications and lose my mind.
rooms.ask: How do you help lower the activation barrier?

opts.t: Offer quiet scaffolding: “Want me to sit next to you while we clear notifications and reply to just one easy item?”
opts.why: Reducing visual clutter and tackling a single micro-step breaks paralysis without taking over.
opts.re: If you just sit there with me... yeah, maybe I can open the inbox.
opts.say: Want me to sit next to you while we clear notifications and reply to just one easy item?

opts.t: “Let's block out two hours and power through the whole queue so you start fresh.”
opts.why: Attempting a marathon catch-up session when depleted invites mid-task burnout.
opts.re: Two hours? I can't even look at it for two minutes without wanting to throw up.
opts.say: Let's block out two hours and power through the whole queue so you start fresh.

opts.t: Shut the laptop: “Then don't look at it. Problem solved for tonight.”
opts.why: Removing presence entirely when work dread is expressed leaves them alone with their backlog.
opts.re: Hey! Don't just shut my laptop like that!

rooms.title: Listening without fixing
rooms.scene: It's 3:15 AM. {P} is staring out the window into the pitch-black yard.
rooms.line: Everything feels completely hollow. Honestly, what's even the point of trying?

opts.t: Acknowledge weight: “That sounds intensely heavy. Can you help me understand what emptiness feels like right now?”
opts.why: Validating existential heaviness and inviting them to expand builds a bridge of trust.
opts.re: It's like... everything I used to care about is just washed out in gray. Thanks for asking instead of telling me to cheer up.
opts.say: That sounds intensely heavy. Can you help me understand what emptiness feels like right now?

opts.t: Sit beside {them}: “I hate hearing you hurt. Let's list three anchors so you see what you have.”
opts.why: Rushing to counter despair with gratitude invalidates acute pain.
opts.re: Don't give me a positivity list right now. It just makes me feel more disconnected.
opts.say: I hate hearing you hurt. Let's list three anchors so you see what you have.

opts.t: Glance at your phone: “It's late. Things always feel bigger at 3 AM—it'll pass.”
opts.why: Looking up unrelated trivia during an existential disclosure communicates complete irrelevance.
opts.re: It's not just 3 AM. It's every hour of every day.

rooms.title: Interruption Subtext
rooms.scene: You're typing at your desk when {p} appears in the doorway, shifting weight and snapping {their} mouth shut.
rooms.line: Hey… are you in the middle of something urgent?

opts.t: Turn around fully: “Never too busy for you. Floor is yours, what's happening?”
opts.why: Instant, unreserved attention tells them they outrank your screen.
opts.re: Oh... I just wanted to ask a small question, but I can come back later if you're working.
opts.say: Never too busy for you. Floor is yours, what's happening?

opts.t: Keep typing while turning halfway: “Wrapping up this paragraph, go ahead and start!”
opts.why: Split attention feels like a polite brush-off.
opts.re: Never mind, it's fine. Keep working.
opts.say: Wrapping up this paragraph, go ahead and start!

opts.t: Keep typing: “Mm-hm. I'm listening, go on.”
opts.why: Saying you're listening while your eyes stay on the screen tells them your work comes first.
opts.re: You're not listening. Forget it. Sorry I bothered you.

rooms.title: Venting vs. Problem-Solving
rooms.scene: Sitting on the sofa, {p} opens up about feeling disconnected from everyone.
rooms.line: I'm surrounded by people, yet I feel like I'm watching life from behind thick glass.

opts.t: Reflect imagery: “That 'behind glass' feeling sounds lonely. Do you want me to sit in that, or brainstorm?”
opts.why: Mirroring metaphors and asking what support they want honors autonomy.
opts.re: Just sit in it with me. I don't need a fix, I just need someone to know how weird it feels.
opts.say: That 'behind glass' feeling sounds lonely. Do you want me to sit in that, or brainstorm?

opts.t: “I get that—let's host a brunch this weekend so you can reconnect!”
opts.why: Prescribing social exposure misses internal dissociation.
opts.re: A brunch? Are you listening to me? That sounds like absolute torture.
opts.say: I get that—let's host a brunch this weekend so you can reconnect!

opts.t: Nod and turn a page: “Everyone feels like that sometimes.”
opts.why: A single perfunctory nod followed by reading closes vulnerability instantly.
opts.re: Yeah, okay. Back to your book.

rooms.title: Crying Without a 'Reason'
rooms.scene: {P} starts crying quietly while folding laundry and tries to wipe the tears away.
rooms.line: Nothing happened today. Why am I crying over nothing? It's embarrassing.
rooms.ask: How do you normalize unprovoked emotion?

opts.t: Sit on the bed: “You don't need a headline tragedy. Sometimes your nervous system just overflows.”
opts.why: Removing the requirement to justify sadness relieves secondary shame.
opts.re: It's just so stupid to cry over folding a towel. Thank you for not making fun of me.
opts.say: You don't need a headline tragedy. Sometimes your nervous system just overflows.

opts.t: Hand {them} a tissue: “Let it out! Crying releases stress hormones so you'll feel lighter.”
opts.why: Promising an immediate mood rebound frames tears as a mechanical cleanse.
opts.re: I don't feel lighter, I just feel broken and exposed. Stop analyzing my tears.
opts.say: Let it out! Crying releases stress hormones so you'll feel lighter.

opts.t: Hand over a clean shirt: “Here, let's just finish the laundry. It'll take your mind off it.”
opts.why: Changing the subject to chores treats their tears like a spill to clean up.
opts.re: Stop handing me laundry like I'm a mess you need to clean up.

rooms.title: Comparing Struggles
rooms.scene: {P} reads a news story on {their} phone and turns guilt inward.
rooms.line: People survive real disasters and I can't handle a normal Tuesday. I'm pathetic.
rooms.ask: How do you counter comparative guilt?

opts.t: Speak steadily: “Other people's pain doesn't shrink yours. Suffering isn't a competition—your struggle is real.”
opts.why: Separating pain from global comparison removes toxic guilt.
opts.re: It's hard to remember that when my brain keeps telling me I'm just weak. But thank you.
opts.say: Other people's pain doesn't shrink yours. Suffering isn't a competition—your struggle is real.

opts.t: “You have a kind heart—let's donate to that cause together to channel that feeling!”
opts.why: Redirecting shame into charity bypasses self-loathing.
opts.re: Donating money doesn't fix the fact that I feel completely useless inside.
opts.say: You have a kind heart—let's donate to that cause together to channel that feeling!

opts.t: Turn the page: “Well, at least you're not dealing with that.”
opts.why: “At least you're not dealing with that” confirms their comparison instead of easing it.
opts.re: Right. Ignore me. I'm just talking nonsense anyway.

rooms.title: Anger Masking Sadness
rooms.scene: Working at the desk, {p} snaps irritably over a misplaced pen, then slumps back looking hollow.
rooms.line: I'm turning into a bitter person. I don't recognize myself.
rooms.ask: How do you read beneath irritability?

opts.t: Keep tone grounded: “Irritability is often exhaustion wearing armor. I know who you are underneath.”
opts.why: Naming irritability as a depletion symptom separates character from condition.
opts.re: I'm sorry I snapped over the pen. I'm just so mad at myself for how useless I've been.
opts.say: Irritability is often exhaustion wearing armor. I know who you are underneath.

opts.t: “Everyone loses patience over small things—put on calming music and let it go.”
opts.why: Minimizing annoyance misses deeper fear about personality changes.
opts.re: Calming music isn't going to fix my brain. Stop trivializing my anger.
opts.say: Everyone loses patience over small things—put on calming music and let it go.

opts.t: Shift your chair away: “Okay. I'll stay out of your way for a bit.”
opts.why: Backing away leaves the tension unaddressed and makes them feel even harder to be around.
opts.re: What is that supposed to mean? Stop judging me.

rooms.title: Numbness Over Sadness
rooms.scene: You ask how {p} feels, and {they} answer{s} with blankness.
rooms.line: I don't even feel sad. Just gray static. Nothing registers.
rooms.ask: How do you respond to emotional blunting?

opts.t: Validate without alarm: “That flat numbness is one of the hardest parts—it's still valid even when it feels like nothing.”
opts.why: Confirming numbness as a recognized symptom reduces panic.
opts.re: It's terrifying when nothing registers at all. Thanks for reminding me I'm not the only one who knows this feeling.
opts.say: That flat numbness is one of the hardest parts—it's still valid even when it feels like nothing.

opts.t: “Let's shake things up—spicy food, a loud movie, something intense to wake your senses!”
opts.why: Trying to shock anhedonia away rarely works.
opts.re: I don't want intense, I want my brain to feel normal. Stop trying to shock me back to life.
opts.say: Let's shake things up—spicy food, a loud movie, something intense to wake your senses!

opts.t: Set your cup down: “Hm. Maybe you're just tired. Want some tea?”
opts.why: Performing a routine action highlights disconnect.
opts.re: Why are you acting like nothing is wrong? I just told you I feel like static.

rooms.title: Fear of Never Recovering
rooms.scene: {P} stands by the window, looking out over the street.
rooms.line: What if this isn't a rough patch? What if this gray version of me is permanent?
rooms.ask: How do you hold hope without toxic positivity?

opts.t: Lean on the railing: “When you're inside the fog, your brain can't picture skies. I'll hold hope for both of us.”
opts.why: Offering to carry hope validates blindness without arguing against pain.
opts.re: I hope you're right. Because right now, I genuinely can't see the other side of this.
opts.say: When you're inside the fog, your brain can't picture skies. I'll hold hope for both of us.

opts.t: “Don't talk like that! Statistics prove almost everyone recovers if you stay positive.”
opts.why: Telling someone to stay positive feels impossible.
opts.re: Being told to stay positive just makes me feel like my pain is my own fault.
opts.say: Don't talk like that! Statistics prove almost everyone recovers if you stay positive.

opts.t: Glance at your watch: “Let's not go down that road tonight. It's getting late.”
opts.why: Checking time communicates impatience with emotional processes.
opts.re: Are you bored of my existential crisis? Go ahead, check the time.

rooms.title: Feeling Unlovable
rooms.scene: Late at night, {p} pulls away slightly from your touch.
rooms.line: I don't know how you stand being around me when I'm like this.
rooms.ask: How do you anchor attachment security?

opts.t: Keep voice steady: “I'm not here because you're effortless—I'm here because I love you in every season.”
opts.why: Affirming love isn't contingent on easy moods counters abandonment fear.
opts.re: Even when I'm like this? ...Thank you. I really needed to hear that tonight.
opts.say: I'm not here because you're effortless—I'm here because I love you in every season.

opts.t: “Because I remember how vibrant you are when healthy, and that version is coming back!”
opts.why: Anchoring love to a past self makes them feel unlovable now.
opts.re: So you love the healthy version of me, not the one sitting here right now.
opts.say: Because I remember how vibrant you are when healthy, and that version is coming back!

opts.t: Withdraw your hand: “Okay. I'll give you some space then.”
opts.why: Complying with a physical pull-away confirms fear that closeness is conditional.
opts.re: Yeah. Figures. You don't want to be close to me either.

rooms.title: Half-Finished Sentences
rooms.scene: {P} starts sharing something personal, pauses, and waves a hand.
rooms.line: Never mind, it sounds stupid out loud. Forget I said anything.
rooms.ask: How do you keep the door open safely?

opts.t: Stay relaxed: “Nothing you feel is stupid. Take your time—or keep it for later, zero pressure.”
opts.why: Reassuring without prying protects psychological safety.
opts.re: Maybe I'll tell you later. Thanks for not making me finish right now.
opts.say: Nothing you feel is stupid. Take your time—or keep it for later, zero pressure.

opts.t: “No, don't shut down—just finish the thought so I can understand!”
opts.why: Pressuring someone to complete thoughts triggers flight.
opts.re: I said forget it! Stop backing me into a corner!
opts.say: No, don't shut down—just finish the thought so I can understand!

opts.t: Turn back to the sink: “Okay, no worries.”
opts.why: Resuming chores immediately signals the moment has passed.
opts.re: Right back to the dishes. Classic.

rooms.title: Crossing into professional territory
rooms.scene: Three weeks of talking at home, and nothing has lifted. {P}'s sleep is broken.
rooms.ask: What is your next evolutionary step?

opts.t: Gently broach options: “We've tried white-knuckling. Want me to help research a counselor we can trust?”
opts.why: Low mood for two weeks signals professional care. Sharing logistics lowers barriers.
opts.re: I'm scared to go, but... yeah. If you help me look, maybe I can do it.
opts.say: We've tried white-knuckling. Want me to help research a counselor we can trust?

opts.t: Leave a folder on the table: “I printed some top therapists and worksheets—look whenever you're ready.”
opts.why: Handing an exhausted person a research packet feels like an exam.
opts.re: What is this? An assignment? You want me to do homework for therapy now?

opts.t: Leave a therapist's card on the table: “This person's supposed to be good. Up to you.”
opts.why: Leaving a card anonymously treats professional help like a pamphlet drop.
opts.re: A business card left on the table? Seriously? You couldn't even talk to me about it?

rooms.title: Defusing Therapy Stigma
rooms.scene: You suggest therapy while sitting together at home.
rooms.line: What if they think I'm completely broken? Or worse, dangerous?
rooms.ask: How do you defuse their panic?

opts.t: Normalize fear: “Seeking a specialist isn't a life sentence. No different than seeing a doctor for a knee injury.”
opts.why: Dismantling stigma with a medical comparison bridges acceptance.
opts.re: When you put it that way... it doesn't sound quite so terrifying. Okay.
opts.say: Seeking a specialist isn't a life sentence. No different than seeing a doctor for a knee injury.

opts.t: “Nobody in our family has to know—we can pay cash and keep it off radar.”
opts.why: Treating therapy like an undercover secret reinforces shame.
opts.re: Keeping it off the radar just makes it sound even more shameful. Is it that bad?
opts.say: Nobody in our family has to know—we can pay cash and keep it off radar.

opts.t: Check your notifications: “I'm sure they've heard worse. You'll be fine.”
opts.why: Checking a device communicates distraction.
opts.re: Yeah, check your notifications. My mental breakdown is interrupting your screen time.

rooms.title: Medication Hesitation
rooms.scene: A doctor recommends an antidepressant; {p} stares at the slip of paper in {their} hands.
rooms.line: If I take pills, am I weak? What if it erases my personality?
rooms.ask: How do you support an informed conversation?

opts.t: Validate concern: “Makes sense to have questions. Want to write worries down to ask the doctor?”
opts.why: Empowering them honors bodily autonomy.
opts.re: I do have a list of side effect fears. Writing them down with you makes me feel less alone.
opts.say: Makes sense to have questions. Want to write worries down to ask the doctor?

opts.t: “Millions take them—just take the first dose tonight to balance chemistry!”
opts.why: Pushing compliance dismisses desire for agency.
opts.re: I'm not swallowing something without talking through my own concerns first!
opts.say: Millions take them—just take the first dose tonight to balance chemistry!

opts.t: Fold the slip into the drawer: “Let's not decide tonight. I'll put it away for now.”
opts.why: Putting the slip away for them bypasses a decision that should be made together.
opts.re: Hey! Don't just file away my prescription without asking me.

rooms.title: The Waitlist Wall
rooms.scene: {P} finally called a counselor, but the earliest appointment is five weeks away. {They} slump{s} against the window.
rooms.line: Five weeks. I knew this was pointless. Maybe I'm just not meant to get help.
rooms.ask: How do you keep the door to help open?

opts.t: Sit beside {them}: “Five weeks is frustrating. Want to get on the waitlist and also check if your doctor can see you sooner?”
opts.why: Validating the setback while offering a second, faster route keeps hope practical instead of preachy.
opts.re: …A doctor sooner? Okay. I didn't think of that. Can you help me call?

opts.t: Smile encouragingly: “Five weeks will fly by! You'll be so busy you won't even notice.”
opts.why: Cheerful minimizing skips the real fear that they'll have to hold on alone until then.
opts.re: Fly by? Every day feels like a month right now.

opts.t: Shrug lightly: “That's how it is everywhere. Maybe just try to tough it out till then.”
opts.why: Telling them to tough it out confirms their fear that help is out of reach.
opts.re: …Right. Tough it out. That's what I've been doing.

rooms.title: The First Appointment Walk
rooms.scene: It's the morning of {p}'s first counseling appointment. {They} stand{s} by the door, coat half on, frozen.
rooms.line: Could you… come with me? Just to the waiting room?

opts.t: Grab your keys: “Of course. I'll sit in the waiting room the whole time and we'll grab a coffee after.”
opts.why: Showing up beside someone for a scary first step lowers the barrier without taking over the appointment.
opts.re: …Thank you. Knowing you're right outside makes this possible.

opts.t: Hesitate: “I'd love to, but you're an adult—you've got this. Text me the second you're done?”
opts.why: Encouraging independence is kind, but it ignores the specific support they asked for at a fragile moment.
opts.re: …Yeah. Sure. I'll text you. If I go.

opts.t: Check the time: “I really can't today. Maybe just reschedule if you're that nervous?”
opts.why: Suggesting they reschedule hands their fear an easy exit.
opts.re: …Maybe I will reschedule. Forget I asked.

rooms.title: First Therapy Session Aftermath
rooms.scene: {P} comes out of an online therapy session, looking drained.
rooms.line: I spent fifty minutes explaining background. I don't feel magically better.
rooms.ask: How do you manage early therapy expectations?

opts.t: Normalize pacing: “Session one is laying the map. Showing up was huge—want to take it easy?”
opts.why: Setting expectations prevents premature dropout.
opts.re: It was exhausting just recounting everything. Thanks for ordering takeout and letting me rest.
opts.say: Session one is laying the map. Showing up was huge—want to take it easy?

opts.t: “Maybe that therapist isn't proactive—should we find someone with action plans?”
opts.why: Jumping to switch therapists undermines rapport.
opts.re: I just finished my first session! Can you give me a second to breathe before grading them?
opts.say: Maybe that therapist wasn't proactive—should we find someone with action plans?

opts.t: Close the door behind them: “Great, that's done then. What's for dinner?”
opts.why: Shutting the door treats therapy as an administrative chore.
opts.re: That's done? Like I just finished a shift at the office. Nice.

rooms.title: Early Signs of Relapse Months Later
rooms.scene: Months later, {p} mentions sleep slipping and gray heaviness returning.
rooms.line: I'm terrified I'm sliding back to square one.
rooms.ask: How do you respond to early warning signs?

opts.t: Stay proactive: “Catching early smoke is wisdom. Let's check with your doctor early.”
opts.why: Treating signs as feedback prevents full relapse.
opts.re: I'm scared it's coming back, but... catching it now is smarter than waiting for a full crash.
opts.say: Catching early smoke is wisdom. Let's check with your doctor early.

opts.t: “Don't overthink bad sleep—you're recovered, stay busy!”
opts.why: Dismissing warning signs delays adjustments.
opts.re: I am telling you the gray is coming back and you're just telling me to ignore it!
opts.say: Don't overthink bad sleep—you're recovered, stay busy!

opts.t: Close your laptop: “Everyone sleeps badly sometimes. You're fine now.”
opts.why: A single nod treats disclosure as routine office closing.
opts.re: I'm fine? You always say that. Like clockwork.

rooms.title: Social Media Spiral
rooms.scene: {P} lies on the sofa doomscrolling for hours.
rooms.line: Everyone else is thriving while I'm rotting under a blanket.
rooms.ask: How do you gently interrupt comparison shame?

opts.t: Offer a soft pivot: “Social media is a brutal highlight reel. Want to put on rain sounds?”
opts.why: Offering environment shifts interrupts loops.
opts.re: Yes, please. My brain was melting scrolling through everyone else's fake lives.
opts.say: Social media is a brutal highlight reel. Want to put on rain sounds?

opts.t: “You need to delete apps—screen time is scientifically proven to worsen depression.”
opts.why: Delivering lectures feels corrective.
opts.re: Don't lecture me about screen-time studies when I'm already feeling miserable.
opts.say: You need to delete apps—screen time is scientifically proven to worsen depression.

opts.t: Walk past the sofa: “Maybe just put the phone down?”
opts.why: Stepping past without interaction leaves isolation.
opts.re: Step right past me with advice. Unreal.

rooms.title: Wanting to Quit Medication
rooms.scene: Three weeks into a new prescription, {p} holds the bottle and frowns.
rooms.line: I feel flat and weird. I'm just going to stop taking these tomorrow.

opts.t: Stay calm: “That sounds really uncomfortable. Can we call your doctor first? Stopping suddenly can make things worse.”
opts.why: Taking side effects seriously while steering decisions back to the prescriber keeps them safe and in control.
opts.re: …Yeah. I didn't know stopping could be bad. Let's call.

opts.t: “You have to give it more time! Just push through—everyone says the first month is the worst.”
opts.why: Pushing them to endure side effects without a doctor dismisses their experience.
opts.re: I don't want to just push through feeling like a zombie.

opts.t: “Your call. Honestly, you did seem more like yourself before the pills anyway.”
opts.why: Undermining treatment can lead to unsafe, sudden stopping.
opts.re: …Really? So maybe I should just stop then.

rooms.title: Telling Work
rooms.scene: {P} has been missing deadlines and needs time for appointments. {They} stare{s} at an empty email to {their} manager.
rooms.line: If I tell them I'm struggling, they'll think I can't do my job.

opts.t: Pull up a chair: “You don't have to share everything. Want to write something short together—just that you need time for medical appointments?”
opts.why: Helping them share only what they choose protects privacy and gets them the time they need.
opts.re: …Just medical appointments. That I can say. Okay, let's write it.

opts.t: “Just be totally honest and tell them everything. Good managers always understand.”
opts.why: Pressuring full disclosure ignores their right to decide what's shared at work.
opts.re: Everything? I'm not ready for my whole office to know.

opts.t: “Maybe don't say anything. They might really start doubting you.”
opts.why: Feeding the fear keeps them stuck without the support they need.
opts.re: …See? Even you think they'd doubt me.

rooms.title: Guarding your sanity
rooms.scene: Carrying the mental load for weeks, you find yourself crying over burnt toast.
rooms.ask: What is the only sustainable survival move?

opts.t: Call a friend and set an evening off for yourself: “I need to vent tonight—are you free?”
opts.why: Caregiver burnout wrecks relationships. Defending boundaries keeps you afloat.
opts.re: I notice you taking time for yourself lately... I'm glad you are. You shouldn't break yourself trying to fix me.

opts.t: Wash your face and quietly take on extra chores: “It's fine. I've got it all handled.”
opts.why: Silent martyrdom ends in collapse.
opts.re: I know you're exhausted because of me. Please stop pretending you're fine.

opts.t: Scrape the burnt toast into the bin: “It's fine. Everything's fine.”
opts.why: Saying “everything's fine” while you quietly fall apart keeps up a rigid facade.
opts.re: Everything's fine? You're cleaning up after me and pretending.

rooms.title: Midnight Crisis Calls
rooms.scene: {P} calls you at 3:00 AM every night. Your work is slipping.
rooms.ask: How do you regulate this dynamic?

opts.t: Set gentle limits: “Let's set check-in times and find a few more people you can call at night.”
opts.why: Sustainable support requires structural parameters.
opts.re: I'm sorry for leaning on you like an all-night hotline. I'll try to use the resources we talked about.

opts.t: Keep your ringer on max: “Call me anytime, day or night. I'll always pick up.”
opts.why: Operating out of raw terror leads to physical collapse.
opts.re: You sound terrified every time I talk to you. I'm ruining your sleep, aren't I?

opts.t: Turn your phone face down: “I really need one night of sleep. Text me in the morning.”
opts.why: Placing the phone face down leaves them stranded without warning.
opts.re: You turned your phone face down? So I'm locked out when I need help most?

rooms.title: Declining an Invitation for Yourself
rooms.scene: A friend invites you out, but {p} looks gloomy.
rooms.line: Go ahead, have fun. I'll stay here in the dark.
rooms.ask: How do you take a healthy break without guilt?

opts.t: Stay warm and clear: “I'm grabbing coffee for ninety minutes, back by four. Love you.”
opts.why: Modeling guilt-free self-care teaches needs coexist safely with love.
opts.re: Go. Have a good time. I'll be here when you get back.
opts.say: I'm grabbing coffee for ninety minutes, back by four. Love you.

opts.t: Cancel quietly: “Actually, I'd rather stay home and keep company.”
opts.why: Sacrificing lifelines breeds unspoken resentment.
opts.re: Don't cancel your plans for me. Now I just feel guilty for ruining your afternoon.
opts.say: Actually, I'd rather stay home and keep company.

opts.t: Grab your jacket: “Okay. Don't wait up.”
opts.why: Leaving with a flat goodbye departs without any reassurance.
opts.re: …Right. Don't wait up. Have fun, I guess.

rooms.title: Bringing in Trusted Family/Friends
rooms.scene: You've been carrying this secret, and {their} sister asks how she can help.
rooms.line: I don't want anyone knowing. Keep this strictly between us.
rooms.ask: How do you encourage widening the circle safely?

opts.t: Respect consent: “I won't share without okay. What if your sister brings dinner by on Thursday?”
opts.why: Honoring confidentiality while introducing low-stakes support reduces isolation.
opts.re: Just dinner? Without a big interrogation? ...Okay, I suppose I can handle that.
opts.say: I won't share without okay. What if your sister brings dinner by on Thursday?

opts.t: Text {their} sister privately: “Just so you know, things have been really hard here.”
opts.why: Breaking confidentiality destroys trust.
opts.re: You went behind my back and told my family? I asked you to keep this between us!

opts.t: Check your calendar: “Sure. I'll just tell her we're busy this month.”
opts.why: Opening schedule apps avoids the relational topic entirely.
opts.re: Checking your schedule while I'm setting a boundary. Awesome.

rooms.title: After a Rough Argument
rooms.scene: Exhaustion boils over; you snap at {p} over a small mess. {P} looks devastated.
rooms.ask: How do you repair the rupture cleanly?

opts.t: Own it without excuses: “Sorry I snapped. I'm stressed, that wasn't fair to you.”
opts.why: Clean repair models emotional maturity.
opts.re: It's okay... I'm hard to live with right now. Thank you for apologizing.
opts.say: Sorry I snapped. I'm stressed, that wasn't fair to you.

opts.t: “Sorry I raised my voice—it's been a lot managing everything while you struggle.”
opts.why: Attaching conditions turns apologies into accusations.
opts.re: There's the dagger. You're sorry, but it's still my fault for struggling.
opts.say: Sorry I raised my voice—it's been a lot managing everything while you struggle.

opts.t: Stand in the doorway: “Let's just not talk about it right now.”
opts.why: Refusing to talk after you snapped leaves the hurt hanging in the air.
opts.re: Not talk about it? You just yelled at me.

rooms.title: Recognizing Your Limits
rooms.scene: {P} asks you to analyze {their} childhood trauma, and you feel out of your depth.
rooms.ask: How do you hold a loving boundary around expertise?

opts.t: Be honest: “I care about hearing this, and want professional skill behind it—can we bring this to your therapist?”
opts.why: Acknowledging limits protects both of you from amateur therapy dynamics.
opts.re: You're right. I shouldn't treat you like my therapist. Let's talk about it in session.
opts.say: I care about hearing this, and want professional skill behind it—can we bring this to your therapist?

opts.t: Try to read the patterns yourself: “Okay, so it sounds like it all goes back to your dad…”
opts.why: Playing amateur psychologist risks unhelpful advice.
opts.re: You sound like you're reading a pop-psychology book at me. That's not helpful.

opts.t: Clear your plate: “That was a long time ago. Maybe it's better to leave it there.”
opts.why: Telling them to leave the past alone shuts down a painful disclosure.
opts.re: Clearing the plate right while I'm talking about trauma. Classy.

rooms.title: Holiday & Family Gathering Pressure
rooms.scene: Before a family dinner, {p} freezes, overwhelmed.
rooms.line: Everyone will ask what I've been doing and I have zero answers.
rooms.ask: How do you co-design an exit strategy?

opts.t: Agree on a signal: “Let's set a 60-minute cap, park unblocked, and if you tap my arm twice, we head home.”
opts.why: Co-creating concrete exit plans restores control.
opts.re: Having an escape plan makes me feel like I can actually walk through that front door.
opts.say: Let's set a 60-minute cap, park unblocked, and if you tap my arm twice, we head home.

opts.t: “Everyone loves you—once you start chatting, your social battery kicks back in!”
opts.why: Predicting spontaneous social recovery dismisses limits.
opts.re: My social battery is dead! Stop pretending this dinner is going to magically cure me.
opts.say: Everyone loves you—once you start chatting, your social battery kicks back in!

opts.t: Check your watch in the mirror: “Just say you've been busy. We need to leave in five.”
opts.why: Checking time places schedule pressure on them.
opts.re: Already timing me before we even leave the house. Great.

rooms.title: Financial Stress Trigger
rooms.scene: An unexpected repair bill arrives in the mail; {p} spirals in panic.
rooms.line: Everything goes wrong when I'm barely holding on. I'm cursed.
rooms.ask: How do you ground catastrophic thinking?

opts.t: Separate math from shame: “This is an annoying car problem, not a failing. Let's look tomorrow.”
opts.why: Containing practical problems prevents global catastrophizing.
opts.re: Okay... we'll look at the numbers tomorrow. Thanks for keeping me from spiraling.
opts.say: This is an annoying car problem, not a failing. Let's look tomorrow.

opts.t: “Don't look—I'll cover the entire thing out of my savings.”
opts.why: Hiding financial reality reinforces incompetence.
opts.re: You're hiding things from me again to protect me. It makes me feel useless.
opts.say: Don't look—I'll cover the entire thing out of my savings.

opts.t: Turn the envelope face down: “Don't look at it tonight. Out of sight, out of mind.”
opts.why: Turning bills face down leaves anxiety hanging.
opts.re: Just sweep the financial disaster under the rug. Perfect.

rooms.title: Anniversary or Trigger Date
rooms.scene: A difficult anniversary is coming up on the calendar.
rooms.ask: How do you acknowledge a quiet trigger date?

opts.t: Check in early: “I know next Tuesday carries heavy memories. Do you want company, distraction, or space?”
opts.why: Naming calendar triggers softly shows attentiveness.
opts.re: Thank you for checking ahead of time. I think I'll need some quiet space that day.
opts.say: I know next Tuesday carries heavy memories. Do you want company, distraction, or space?

opts.t: Plan a surprise outing for that day: “Keep Tuesday free—I've got a fun surprise planned!”
opts.why: Ambushing someone on trauma anniversaries misfires.
opts.re: Why did you ambush me with a party on this specific day? You didn't even check!

opts.t: Turn the calendar page: “New month already. Time flies.”
opts.why: Brushing past the date avoids acknowledging what it means to them.
opts.re: Flipping past the date like it's nothing. You don't even remember.

rooms.title: Quiet Resentment
rooms.scene: You catch yourself feeling resentful that your life has shrunk to caregiving—and then instantly guilty for feeling it.
rooms.ask: What do you do with that feeling?

opts.t: Admit it to yourself and a friend: “I love them, and I'm worn out. Both are true. I need some support too.”
opts.why: Naming resentment early, without shame, stops it from leaking out in hurtful ways later.
opts.re: You've seemed so tired lately… I'm glad you're talking to someone too.

opts.t: Push it down: “I'm not allowed to feel this. They're the one who's struggling.”
opts.why: Burying the feeling doesn't make it go away—it builds pressure until it bursts.
opts.re: Are you okay? You seem a bit far away lately.

opts.t: Mutter while tidying: “Must be nice to have someone doing everything for you.”
opts.why: Letting resentment out as sarcasm wounds the person who already feels like a burden.
opts.re: …I'm sorry. I know I'm a burden. I'm really sorry.

rooms.title: The ultimate midnight test
rooms.scene: Late at night, in the shadows, {p} speaks in a flat tone.
rooms.line: Sometimes I honestly believe everyone would be better off if I vanished permanently.

opts.t: Stay grounded and ask: “Are you having active thoughts of ending your life?”
opts.why: Asking directly does not plant suicidal ideas; it breaks secrecy and opens urgent help.
opts.re: Yes... I am. I'm so tired, and I don't know how to keep going.
opts.say: Are you having active thoughts of ending your life?

opts.t: Wrap {them} in an embrace: “Don't think that, let's put on a movie.”
opts.why: Diverting away from suicidal cues sweeps crisis under the carpet.
opts.re: You're not listening to me. I'm telling you I want to disappear!
opts.say: Don't think that, let's put on a movie.

opts.t: Pull the blanket up: “Don't say things like that. Let's just get some sleep.”
opts.why: Turning away into blankets meets suicidal ideation with literal darkness.
opts.re: You're just going to turn away? I'm not talking about sleep.

rooms.title: Subtle Warning Signs
rooms.scene: You notice {p} giving away {their} books and seeming strangely serene.
rooms.ask: How do you interpret this abrupt shift?

opts.t: Check in directly: “I noticed you're giving away things and seem quiet. Are you safe, or having thoughts of ending life?”
opts.why: Sudden calm can signal a resolved plan; direct inquiry is vital.
opts.re: I... yes. I was getting rid of things because I didn't think I'd need them anymore. Thank you for asking.
opts.say: I noticed you're giving away things and seem quiet. Are you safe, or having thoughts of ending life?

opts.t: Smile at the boxes: “I'm so glad your mood finally lifted! Decluttering is great for peace of mind.”
opts.why: Mistaking warning signs for recovery delays life-saving care.
opts.re: You completely misread this. I'm not feeling peaceful, I'm giving up.

opts.t: Step past the donation box: “Nice, more space. Need help carrying those out?”
opts.why: Stepping past behavioral warning indicators ignores risk shifts.
opts.re: You didn't even notice what I was packing away, or why.

rooms.title: The Goodbye Text
rooms.scene: Late at night, your phone lights up with a text from {p}: “Thank you for everything. Please take care of yourself.”
rooms.ask: Something feels wrong. What do you do?

opts.t: Go to {them} right away and ask gently but directly: “Your text scared me. Are you thinking about ending your life?”
opts.why: Messages that sound like goodbyes are a warning sign. Asking directly opens the door to urgent help.
opts.re: …Yes. I didn't know how else to say it. I'm so tired. Please don't go.

opts.t: Reply by text: “Aww, love you too! Get some sleep, okay?”
opts.why: Treating a possible goodbye as a sweet message misses a serious warning sign.
opts.re: …Yeah. Okay. Goodnight.

opts.t: Decide to deal with it tomorrow: “They're probably just being dramatic tonight.”
opts.why: Dismissing a goodbye message can leave someone alone at the most dangerous moment.
opts.re: …I guess nobody's coming.

rooms.title: No Future
rooms.scene: Sitting on the edge of the bed, {p} speaks in a calm, tired voice.
rooms.line: I don't see a future anymore. I can't picture next month at all.

opts.t: Sit close and ask clearly: “That sounds incredibly heavy. When you say no future, are you having thoughts of ending your life?”
opts.why: Hopelessness about the future can be linked to suicidal thoughts. Asking plainly shows you can handle the answer.
opts.re: …Sometimes. More than sometimes. I'm scared of how much I think about it.

opts.t: “Of course there's a future! We've got that trip next summer—focus on that.”
opts.why: Rushing to argue with hopelessness skips over finding out how much danger they're in.
opts.re: You're not hearing me. I can't even picture tomorrow.

opts.t: “Everyone feels that way sometimes. Try to get some sleep.”
opts.why: Brushing off hopelessness as normal tiredness can leave serious thoughts unspoken.
opts.re: …Right. Sleep. Sure.

rooms.title: Sudden Calm
rooms.scene: After weeks of struggle, {p} suddenly seems peaceful, has stopped taking {their} medication, and keeps saying everything is “sorted out” now.

opts.t: Gently check in: “You seem really different tonight. I need to ask—are you thinking about killing yourself?”
opts.why: A sudden calm after a long struggle, especially with stopping treatment, can be a sign of a decision. Asking directly is vital.
opts.re: …I didn't think anyone would notice. Yes. I've been thinking about it a lot.

opts.t: “You seem so much calmer! I'm proud of you for sorting things out.”
opts.why: Mistaking a warning sign for recovery can delay life-saving help.
opts.re: …Yeah. Everything's sorted. Don't worry about me.

opts.t: Let it go: “Good. Finally a quiet night for both of us.”
opts.why: Feeling relieved instead of curious can mean missing the most important moment to ask.
opts.re: …Yeah. A quiet night.

rooms.title: Imminent Safety Action
rooms.scene: {P} confirms those dark intentions.

opts.t: Thank {them}, stay right beside {them} and call crisis professionals: “Thank you for telling me. I'm not leaving. We're getting help right now.”
opts.why: Imminent risks require professional intervention. Never carry crisis alone.
opts.re: Thank you for staying... don't let me go.

opts.t: Talk until {they} seem{s} calmer: “Let's just talk tonight, and I'll send you a hotline number for the morning.”
opts.why: Handing off crisis management leaves vulnerability exposed overnight.
opts.re: Don't hand me a link for tomorrow. I need help right now!

opts.t: Sit still on the edge of the bed: “I… I don't know what to say. Let's talk about it tomorrow.”
opts.why: Remaining motionless fails to initiate emergency safety protocols.
opts.re: Tomorrow? I need help now. Please, do something!

rooms.title: Please Don't Tell
rooms.scene: {P} grips your sleeve after admitting {their} thoughts.
rooms.line: Please don't tell anyone. Promise me. I'll be fine.

opts.t: Hold {their} hand: “I love you too much to keep this secret. I'm staying with you, and we're calling a crisis line together right now.”
opts.why: Safety comes before secrecy. Staying close and getting professional help is an act of love, not betrayal.
opts.re: …I'm scared. But… okay. Don't let go of my hand.

opts.t: “Okay, I won't tell anyone—but promise me you'll call someone tomorrow.”
opts.why: Agreeing to secrecy and waiting until tomorrow leaves them alone with the danger tonight.
opts.re: …Tomorrow. Sure. I promise.

opts.t: “Fine, I promise. Let's just never talk about this again.”
opts.why: Promising silence leaves them carrying something deadly alone.
opts.re: …Okay. Never again.

rooms.title: Fine By Morning
rooms.scene: {P} wipes {their} face and tries to brush it off.
rooms.line: Honestly, I'm okay now. You can go to sleep. I'll be fine by morning.

opts.t: Stay put: “I'm not going anywhere tonight. Let's call a crisis line together and get some help for right now.”
opts.why: Thoughts of suicide can come back fast. Staying close and getting support tonight matters more than sleep.
opts.re: …You'd really stay? …Okay. I didn't want to be alone anyway.

opts.t: “Okay… but leave your door open and wake me if anything changes.”
opts.why: Checking in is caring, but it still leaves them alone at the riskiest time.
opts.re: …Sure. I'll wake you. Goodnight.

opts.t: “Okay, if you say so. Goodnight.”
opts.why: Taking a quick “I'm fine” at face value after a crisis leaves them on their own.
opts.re: …Goodnight.

rooms.title: Making the Room Safer
rooms.scene: While you're waiting for the crisis line to answer, you remember there are medications and other things in the house {p} could use to hurt {themselves}.

opts.t: Gently say: “While we wait, I'm going to put some things away for tonight, just to keep you safe. I'm right here.”
opts.why: Putting dangerous things out of reach during a crisis is one of the most effective ways to keep someone safe.
opts.re: …Okay. I… I think that's a good idea. Thank you.

opts.t: Decide not to bring it up: “Mentioning it might upset them more.”
opts.why: Avoiding the topic to keep the peace leaves dangerous things within reach.
opts.re: …Is someone answering? I'm so tired.

opts.t: Leave the room to make tea: “I'll just be in the kitchen for a bit, okay?”
opts.why: Leaving someone alone in a crisis, with dangerous things nearby, puts them at serious risk.
opts.re: …You're leaving? Please don't leave me alone right now.

rooms.title: On the Crisis Line
rooms.scene: The crisis line counselor answers. {P} freezes, phone shaking in {their} hand.
rooms.line: I can't… I don't know what to say to them.

opts.t: Sit close: “You don't have to say it perfectly. Want me to start, and you add what you can?”
opts.why: Helping them begin the conversation lowers the barrier while keeping their voice in it.
opts.re: …Okay. You start. I'll try. Stay right here.

opts.t: Take the phone and explain everything yourself while {they} sit{s} silently.
opts.why: Taking over completely gets help moving, but they may feel talked about instead of supported.
opts.re: …You told them everything. I feel like a case file.

opts.t: “Maybe this was too much. Let's just hang up and try tomorrow.”
opts.why: Hanging up in the middle of a crisis closes the door on help that's right there.
opts.re: …Tomorrow. Okay. Maybe I'm not worth the call anyway.

setbacks.title: The Nonlinear Zigzag
setbacks.scene: After a few good days, {p} wakes up and can't get out of bed.
setbacks.line: I thought I was fixed. I ruined progress overnight.
setbacks.ask: How do you frame this setback?

opts.t: “Recovery is a messy zigzag, not a straight line. One heavy morning doesn't erase hard work.”
opts.why: Normalizing nonlinear healing halts all-or-nothing spirals.
opts.re: It feels like stepping backward a million miles. But... maybe you're right.
opts.say: Recovery is a messy zigzag, not a straight line. One heavy morning doesn't erase hard work.

opts.t: “Look how strong you were—you proved you can beat this, let's push through!”
opts.why: Using recent good days turns a dip into a performance failure.
opts.re: Stop throwing my past good days in my face. Today sucks!
opts.say: Look how strong you were—you proved you can beat this, let's push through!

opts.t: Set the alarm as usual: “Let's just treat it like a normal day. You'll feel better once you're up.”
opts.why: Proceeding with standard schedule mechanics treats the day as normal.
opts.re: Turning on my alarm like it's a normal day. You don't get it at all.

setbacks.title: Skipping Therapy
setbacks.scene: {P} panicked and skipped therapy, and now sits alone outside.
setbacks.line: I drove to the parking lot, panicked, and drove home. I'm a coward.
setbacks.ask: How do you respond to the avoidance loop?

opts.t: “Starting is terrifying. Want me to sit beside you while we reschedule?”
opts.why: Lowering the activation barrier keeps momentum alive.
opts.re: I sat in the parking lot and just panicked. But yes... please help me call.
opts.say: Starting is terrifying. Want me to sit beside you while we reschedule?

opts.t: “Driving to the lot is huge progress! Promise me next week we won't let fear win.”
opts.why: Extracting a promise adds performance pressure.
opts.re: Don't make me promise anything. I failed today.
opts.say: Driving to the lot is huge progress! Promise me next week we won't let fear win.

opts.t: Hang up your keys: “Okay. Well, there's always next week.”
opts.why: “There's always next week” skips over how scared and ashamed they feel right now.
opts.re: Next week? You didn't even ask why I came right back home.

rooms.title: Admitting it to yourself
rooms.scene: You've cancelled plans three weekends in a row and spend evenings on the couch. {P} sits down next to you.
rooms.line: Hey… you've seemed really tired. How are you doing — really?

opts.t: Take a breath: “Not great, actually. I think I've been running on empty.”
opts.why: Admitting truth to someone who cares is the first step.
opts.re: Thank you for telling me the truth. We'll take it slow, together.
opts.say: Not great, actually. I think I've been running on empty for a while, and I didn't want to admit it.

opts.t: “Just dealing with a mental backlog from work, I'll fix it this week.”
opts.why: Intellectualizing exhaustion keeps you in your head.
opts.re: A plan's good… but how are you feeling, not just your work?
opts.say: Just dealing with a massive mental backlog from work, but I'll fix it this week.

opts.t: “Nothing.”
opts.why: A flat denial cuts off connection instantly.
opts.re: …Okay. I'm here if that changes.
opts.say: Nothing.

rooms.title: Naming What You Need
rooms.scene: You catch your reflection in the mirror. {P} watches from the doorway.
rooms.line: Want company, or would you rather be alone?

opts.t: “Company, I think. You don't have to say anything—just sit with me?”
opts.why: Naming small needs makes it easy to help.
opts.re: Of course. I'm right here. No words needed.
opts.say: Company, I think. You don't have to say anything—just sit with me?

opts.t: “Stay if you want, but I'm staring at my phone so don't expect good company.”
opts.why: Disclaimers prevent real connection.
opts.re: That's okay. I'll just sit with you, phone and all.
opts.say: Stay if you want, but I'm staring at my phone so don't expect good company.

opts.t: Pull your hood down: “Doesn't matter. Whatever you want.”
opts.why: Adjusting garments to block eye contact shuts off bridge building.
opts.re: …Okay. I'll be nearby if you need me.

rooms.title: Recognizing the Pattern
rooms.scene: Your morning alarm goes off; dread hits instantly.

opts.t: Notice honestly: “This isn't laziness—I'm carrying a heavy fog, I'll take it gently today.”
opts.why: Recognizing symptoms stops morning self-attack.
opts.re: You're being gentle with yourself today. I'm really glad.
opts.say: This isn't laziness—I'm carrying a heavy fog, I'll take it gently today.

opts.t: “I lack discipline—if I force a cold shower and five tasks, I'll snap out.”
opts.why: Treating depletion as a willpower deficit crashes.
opts.re: Hey… maybe go easy today? A cold shower won't fix tired.
opts.say: I lack discipline—if I force a cold shower and five tasks, I'll snap out.

opts.t: Switch the alarm off: “Five more minutes. I'll deal with today later.”
opts.why: Silencing alarms initiates unannounced retreat.
opts.re: Rough morning? I'll bring you some water.

rooms.title: Dropping the 'Fine' Reflex
rooms.scene: A friend texts asking how you are; your thumbs type 'All good!'.
rooms.ask: Before hitting send, what do you adjust?

opts.t: Delete the reflex: “Honestly, a bit wiped out lately—low on energy, but glad you checked.”
opts.why: Replacing masking with truth keeps connection alive.
opts.re: I'm glad you told them the truth. That's real connection.
opts.say: Honestly, a bit wiped out lately—low on energy, but glad you checked.

opts.t: Send 'All good!' for now: “I'll tell them the real stuff later—no need to bring the mood down.”
opts.why: Waiting for 100% creates exile.
opts.re: Maybe tell them a little more later? They'd want to know.

opts.t: Tap send: “All good! Super busy, you know how it is.”
opts.why: Submitting masking phrases deepens isolation.
opts.re: …Who was that? You look miles away.

rooms.title: Sitting With Unexplained Sadness
rooms.scene: You sit in the armchair for twenty minutes, unable to move.

opts.t: Breathe without judgment: “It's okay that transitions feel heavy. I'll get up when ready.”
opts.why: Granting permission to pause removes secondary stress.
opts.re: Take your time. I'll be right here when you're ready.
opts.say: It's okay that transitions feel heavy. I'll get up when ready.

opts.t: Open some motivational videos: “Come on—get hyped, get up, get moving.”
opts.why: Artificial hype ignores genuine exhaustion.
opts.re: Hey, no hype needed. It's okay to just rest.

opts.t: Keep staring at the wall: “It doesn't matter. Nothing's going to change anyway.”
opts.why: Staring blankly burns time without progress.
opts.re: …Hey. Want me to sit with you?

rooms.title: Body & Exhaustion
rooms.scene: You notice self-disgust creeping in over skipped meals and exercise.
rooms.ask: How do you respond to your inner critic?

opts.t: Shift to basic care: “My body isn't failing—it's on reserve fuel. Water and a simple snack.”
opts.why: Meeting energy levels rebuilds self-trust.
opts.re: Reserve fuel. I like that. Here — water and some crackers.
opts.say: My body isn't failing—it's on reserve fuel. Water and a simple snack.

opts.t: Plan a big reset: “Tomorrow: 6 AM start, strict 30-day plan. No excuses.”
opts.why: All-or-nothing plans collapse.
opts.re: Thirty days at 6 AM? Maybe start with one small thing.

opts.t: Turn away from the mirror: “Why bother. It's not like it makes a difference.”
opts.why: Averting gaze avoids reality.
opts.re: …Hey, come eat something with me?

rooms.title: Separating Identity from Mood
rooms.scene: Staring at a project on your desk, you feel total indifference.

opts.t: Remind gently: “Losing interest is a symptom of burnout, not proof I've lost myself.”
opts.why: Separating temporary anhedonia preserves hope.
opts.re: That's not losing yourself. That's just tired. I still see you.
opts.say: Losing interest is a symptom of burnout, not proof I've lost myself.

opts.t: Push on anyway: “Three hours, no breaks. I can't afford to lose my edge.”
opts.why: Grinding creates aversion.
opts.re: Three hours? Please take a break too.

opts.t: Close the project: “I used to love this. Guess that version of me is gone.”
opts.why: Closing workspace windows severs connection.
opts.re: …Want to take a break together?

rooms.title: When Someone Notices
rooms.scene: {P} mentions that you've been quiet all week.
rooms.line: No pressure, I just miss your voice.

opts.t: “Thanks for noticing gently. My brain has been foggy—nothing you did.”
opts.why: Reassuring prevents misunderstandings.
opts.re: Thank you for telling me. I was worried it was me.
opts.say: Thanks for noticing gently. My brain has been foggy—nothing you did.

opts.t: “Just thinking through work logistics, I'll be normal Friday.”
opts.why: Hiding behind work blocks support.
opts.re: Okay… but I'm here if it's more than work.
opts.say: Just thinking through work logistics, I'll be normal Friday.

opts.t: Push your plate away: “I'm fine. Just not hungry.”
opts.why: Shifting plates terminates meal engagement.
opts.re: …Okay. I'll let you eat.

rooms.title: Letting Go of 'Shoulds'
rooms.scene: Looking at today's errand list, you completed zero.
rooms.ask: What is the healthiest end-of-day move?

opts.t: Cross off items, rest: “Surviving a heavy day counts as enough today.”
opts.why: Recalibrating expectations prevents shame spirals.
opts.re: Surviving counts. I'm proud of you for today.
opts.say: Surviving a heavy day counts as enough today.

opts.t: Open the list again: “If I stay up till 2 AM, I can still get all of it done.”
opts.why: Sacrificing sleep worsens mood regulation.
opts.re: 2 AM? Please sleep. The list will still be there.

opts.t: Fold the list in half: “Another useless day. Typical.”
opts.why: Creasing uncompleted lists stores failure away.
opts.re: …Want to talk about it?

rooms.title: Admitting You Need Help
rooms.scene: You realize you've been white-knuckling it alone for a month.

opts.t: Acknowledge quietly: “I can't willpower my way out—needing support doesn't mean I failed.”
opts.why: Accepting support is the turning point.
opts.re: Needing support isn't failing. I'm so glad you see that.
opts.say: I can't willpower my way out—needing support doesn't mean I failed.

opts.t: Set yourself a deadline: “Three more months. If it's still bad then, I'll get help.”
opts.why: Arbitrary delays prolong suffering.
opts.re: Three months is a long time to hurt. I'm here whenever.

opts.t: Switch off the lamp: “I got myself into this. I'll get myself out.”
opts.why: Switching off lights maintains solo endurance.
opts.re: …Goodnight. I'm right here.

rooms.title: Accepting small help
rooms.scene: {P} sets a plate of toast down beside you.
